batch: B (legal and travel: Indonesian marriage law, Australian side, entry rules, Bali levy, Smartraveller)
method_note: FAST mode, one round. F-100 to F-112 reused, each keeping its original checked date (2026-11-13 from the marriage-licence-validity and wedding-witnesses packs; 2026-11-16 from the getting-married-in-germany B pack, itself carried from France and Jamaica). 'Wedded Advisor confirms' wording removed; each legal fact now names the authority. F-113 to F-126 new, read in full today via Apify web-fetch (direct WebFetch to embassy.gov.au and smartraveller.gov.au is blocked in this session): indonesia.embassy.gov.au/jakt/MarriageInd.html, smartraveller.gov.au/destinations/asia/indonesia and lovebali.baliprov.go.id/faq. peraturan.bpk.go.id returned HTTP 503, so Law No. 1 of 1974 is cited through the Embassy page only. Brand facts about Bali resorts in the honeymoon-planner and travel-advisor packs were not reused: they belong to batch A. No competitor, aggregator or site/ draft used.

facts.claim: Indonesia (including Bali): an Australian marrying in Indonesia applies for a Certificate of No Impediment (CNI) from the Australian Embassy in Jakarta or a Consulate-General; Bali, NTB and NTT fall under the Australian Consulate-General in Bali. The local Civil Registry Office or KUA normally requires the CNI from the mission with jurisdiction.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Re-read today (F-113 to F-118): unchanged. The Embassy says to check with the Civil Registry Office or KUA which mission to attend. Confirmed by the Australian Consulate-General Bali and the Civil Registry Office (Catatan Sipil) where the marriage will take place.

facts.claim: Indonesia: 'We do not place an expiry date on the CNI, however the local Civil Registry Office do not normally accept CNIs that were issued more than 3 months prior.'
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Wording unchanged on today's read. Write 'plan on a CNI issued within 3 months of the wedding'. The 3-month figure is Civil Registry practice, not law; confirm with the Civil Registry Office in the regency where you marry.

facts.claim: Indonesia: for non-Muslim marriages, couples lodge a Notice of Intention to Marry with the Civil Registry Office at least 10 days before the wedding, and the marriage must be registered there afterwards to be legal. Both parties must hold the same religion recognised by the Indonesian Government (Law No. 1 of 1974). A CNI is usually issued while you wait if documents are complete.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: The Embassy calls this 'a general guide only' and says requirements vary by province. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office (Dinas Kependudukan dan Pencatatan Sipil) in the area of the wedding.

facts.claim: Indonesia: Government Regulation (PP) No. 9 of 1975, implementing Marriage Law No. 1 of 1974, article 10: following the procedure of each religion or belief, the marriage takes place before the Registrar (Pegawai Pencatat) and is attended by two witnesses ('dihadiri oleh dua orang saksi').
facts.publisher: Badan Pemeriksa Keuangan RI (Indonesian Audit Board) legal database
facts.use_note: Medium: article text confirmed via search excerpts in the original pack, not read in full on BPK. States the number of witnesses only; no age, ID or relationship rule from an official source (N-104). Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office in Bali.

facts.claim: DFAT notarial fees from 1 January 2026, in Australian dollars: Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage AUD 181; document legalisation by Apostille AUD 105. Fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year.
facts.use_note: Write 'from AUD 181 (2026 DFAT fee)' for a CNI issued in Australia. Medium for Bali: the Embassy Indonesia marriage page gives no CNI fee, and the fee charged at the Consulate-General Bali (possibly in IDR) was not read (N-102). Re-check after 1 January 2027.

facts.claim: How to apply for a CNI through DFAT: complete the CNI application form, signing it only in front of an authorised witness (in Australia a Justice of the Peace, or an Australian Passports official at your appointment; overseas a consular official). If the overseas authority wants documents legalised, also complete a Document Legalisation Request Form. Submit by mail or in person and pay on submission. Incomplete applications are not processed. DFAT advises checking whether the CNI must be issued in the country of marriage, in which case the Australian embassy there can issue it.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: Confidence restored to high for Indonesia (it was lowered only for Germany). For Bali it fits F-100: the Civil Registry normally wants the CNI from the mission with jurisdiction, i.e. the Consulate-General Bali, which issues it usually while you wait.

facts.claim: You cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia. Australia does not recognise overseas marriages where either person was already married, not old enough, too closely related, or forced to marry. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage, but may not be usable as proof of a name change; check with your state or territory BDM registry.
facts.use_note: Matches the Embassy Indonesia FAQ (F-117). Confirmed by DFAT; for name change use, the state or territory BDM registry.

facts.claim: The Attorney-General's Department says overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant or registered in Australia, and an overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid in the overseas country and would have been valid here. Some states and territories do not accept overseas marriage certificates for a change of name. Legal basis: Marriage Act 1961, Part VA.
facts.use_note: An Australian celebrant cannot legally marry a couple in Bali; a Bali ceremony led by an Australian celebrant is symbolic unless the Indonesian legal process (F-102) is also followed.

facts.claim: Passport name change after marriage: for a new passport you must link the new name to your Australian birth or citizenship certificate with an Australian RBDM marriage certificate, registered relationship certificate, or RBDM name change certificate. The Passport Office always requires an RBDM name change certificate if you were born in Australia and married overseas. Foreign certificates are accepted only if you cannot get an Australian equivalent, must be legalised, and non-English documents must be translated in full by an approved translation service.
facts.publisher: Australian Passport Office, Change of name or gender
facts.use_note: An Indonesian Civil Registry marriage certificate is in Bahasa Indonesia; its format and any bilingual version were not checked (N-105). Confirmed by the Australian Passport Office and the state BDM registry.

facts.claim: Legal at home, celebration abroad: Australia has no marriage licence; the formal step is giving a Notice of Intended Marriage (NOIM) to an authorised celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding. Since 12 June 2024 the NOIM can be witnessed remotely by audio-visual link, and a couple outside Australia can complete it with an authorised witness overseas (such as an Australian consular officer or a notary public, not a celebrant).
facts.use_note: Key for Bali packages: many couples sign legally at home and hold a symbolic ceremony in Bali, which avoids the same-religion rule (F-114). Present as an option, not advice.

facts.claim: Since 12 June 2024 the authorised celebrant must meet separately and in person with each party before the marriage, and must be physically present to solemnise it, together with the couple and 2 witnesses over 18. There are no video-link weddings.

Smartraveller's essentials checklist says to confirm your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond the end of your trip; some countries and airlines apply a six-month validity rule, it can apply when transiting, and getting it wrong can mean being stranded.
facts.use_note: For Indonesia the country page states a specific 6-month rule (F-120); prefer that.

facts.claim: Allow at least 6 weeks to get a passport; where possible, don't book flights without a valid passport; faster processing may be available for urgent travel at an extra fee.

Australian Embassy Indonesia: 'Generally, Indonesian nationals, and persons of any other nationality may marry in Indonesia provided they hold a religion recognised by the Indonesian Government (Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism or Christian). Under the Indonesian Marriage Law, marriages may be performed by Ministers of Religion, officers of the Civil Registry Office (Kantor Catatan Sipil) or the Office of Religious Affairs (Kantor Urusan Agama). For a marriage to be legal, it must be conducted according to the religion and conform to the laws of the countries of the parties involved.'
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Quote as the Embassy's 'general guide only'. Medium because the religion list is the Embassy's short form; the Indonesian Government's own list was not read (N-101), so do not state a number of recognised religions. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office (Catatan Sipil) where the marriage takes place, or the Indonesian Embassy or Consulate-General in Australia.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia, 'Couples must be of the same religion': 'Under Indonesian Law No.1 of 1974 concerning marriage (the 'Marriage Law'), both parties must hold the same religion, if not, one party must convert to the other religion.'
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Answers the brief's question: yes, per the Australian Embassy's reading of Law No. 1 of 1974, both partners must share a recognised religion for a legal Indonesian marriage. The statute text itself was not read (peraturan.bpk.go.id returned 503; N-100). Do not repeat the Embassy's 'anecdotal' remark about conversion. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office and the Australian Consulate-General Bali.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia, Other Weddings: for non-Muslim marriages (Christian, Hindu, etc.), couples lodge a Notice of Intention to Marry with the Civil Registry Office at least 10 days before the wedding; after the ceremony the marriage must be registered at the Civil Registry Office to be legal. Both applicants need originals and photocopies of: the CNI from the Embassy or Consulate-General; passports or KTP; birth certificates; marriage certificate; proof of dissolution of a previous marriage or death certificate of a former partner (if applicable); four photos (4x6cm) of the couple. Requirements can vary from province to province, so check with the Civil Registry Office where you will marry first.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: This is the civil registration (Catatan Sipil, now Dinas Kependudukan dan Pencatatan Sipil, Dukcapil) step for foreigners as the Embassy states it. 'Marriage certificate' appears in the list as written; its meaning is unclear (likely the religious certificate), so omit it or say 'the documents your Civil Registry Office lists'. No Dukcapil page was read (N-100). Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office of the regency where you marry.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia, Islamic Weddings: Muslim weddings are performed by the Office of Religious Affairs (Kantor Urusan Agama), which issues the Marriage Book (Buku Nikah) as evidence of the marriage. There is usually no requirement to register such a marriage with the Civil Registry Office, but a Civil Registry Marriage Certificate is recommended if you intend to relocate to another country.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Short mention only. Confirmed by the local KUA.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia FAQ: you cannot marry at the Embassy or Consulate-General; a CNI is usually issued while you wait if documents are correct and complete; since 1 January 1995 any legally performed overseas marriage that would have been legal in Australia is accepted as a legal marriage under Australian law; you do not register the marriage with the Embassy, and cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia; you cannot marry before a divorce decree absolute is issued.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Consistent with F-106 and F-107. Confirmed by the Australian Consulate-General Bali.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia: 'Neither DFAT nor its missions overseas can advise on other countries' specific requirements for Australians to get married overseas.' For current requirements contact the nearest Indonesian Embassy or Consulate-General or the Indonesian Civil Registry Office (Catatan Sipil) where the marriage will take place. Couples make their own arrangements with the religious minister and/or civil registry celebrants, and are advised to talk to a lawyer in Australia and/or Indonesia. It can be difficult for foreigners without Indonesian language skills to liaise with the Civil Registry Office and celebrants, and the Embassy suggests engaging a Wedding Organiser if unsure.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Useful, sourced support for why a package with a local wedding organiser helps with paperwork. Do not imply the Embassy endorses any organiser. Contact email on the page is obfuscated; link the page instead.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Indonesia overall advice: 'Exercise a high degree of caution in Indonesia overall due to security risks. Higher levels apply in some areas.' Page shows 'Updated: 21 October 2026' and 'Still current at: 18 November 2026'. The higher levels ('Reconsider your need to travel') relate to areas in Papua, not Bali. Smartraveller also warns of methanol poisoning, including in Bali and Lombok.
facts.use_note: Level 2 of 4. Medium only because the exact list of higher-level areas was not extracted in full; the Papua attribution is from the security section read today. 'Still current at 18 November' reflects the page's time zone. Advice levels change; link the page and say 'at the time of writing'. Methanol warning matters for guest bar packages; avoid alarmist tone.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Indonesia entry: before arriving at international entry points you need to complete an arrival card and apply for an e-Visa on Arrival (e-VOA), both on the All Indonesia website (allindonesia.imigrasi.go.id). If travelling for tourism you can apply for an e-VOA online at least 48 hours before travel via the Directorate General of Immigration e-Visa website or All Indonesia; otherwise you can still apply for a regular VOA at certain international airports, seaports and land crossings, where some checkpoints may only accept cash. The e-VOA and VOA cost IDR 500,000, with the e-VOA also charging a small online processing fee. They are valid for a 30-day stay and can be extended once (for a maximum of 30 days) at an immigration office, within the first 30 days. You need at least 6 months passport validity from the date you plan to enter and leave Indonesia, and a return or onward flight booking.
facts.use_note: Guest-facing travel fact. IDR amount is an official fee, not an AUD price; do not convert to AUD without a sourced rate. Smartraveller notes the arrival card is completed within 72 hours (3 days) of travel. Warn readers to use only the official imigrasi.go.id sites. Indonesian immigration pages not read directly (N-103).

facts.claim: Smartraveller Indonesia: 'Foreign tourists entering Bali must pay a tourist levy of IDR 150,000 per person. The tourist levy is separate from the e-Visa on Arrival (e-VOA) or the Visa on Arrival (VOA).' Cashless payment online before travel or at designated counters at Bali's airport and seaport; transit passengers and some visa holders may be exempt.
facts.use_note: Matches the Bali Provincial Government (F-122).

facts.claim: Bali Provincial Government, Love Bali FAQ: 'Foreign Tourists levy are subject to Rp 150,000 per person.' It is paid only once while travelling in Bali, before leaving Indonesia, cashless only: via the Love Bali system before entering Bali, at payment counters at Bali's airport and port, or at registered endpoints (hotels, travel agents, tourist attractions). Proof of payment is a levy voucher with a QR code sent by email. Accepted: Visa, Mastercard, American Express and JCB credit cards, bank transfer, Virtual Account, UnionPay and QRIS. Exemptions include diplomatic and official visas, transport crew, KITAS or KITAP holders, family unification, student, golden and other visas. Legal basis includes Law No. 15 of 2023 on Bali Province and Bali Provincial Regulation No. 2 of 2025 amending Regulation No. 6 of 2023 on the Foreign Tourists Levy.
facts.publisher: Bali Provincial Government (Pemerintah Provinsi Bali), Love Bali
facts.use_note: Primary source for the levy; state 'IDR 150,000 per person, paid once' and link lovebali.baliprov.go.id. Not an AUD price; no AUD conversion sourced. Useful line for guest information packs. New domain added to domains.md.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Indonesia: weather conditions can change quickly during the wet season, usually around October to April; the wet season can be different in Eastern Indonesia, where it usually runs from April to August. Flooding, landslides and mudslides occur regularly during the wet season; walking and driving in flooded areas is dangerous; regularly check weather reports.
facts.use_note: Bali is not Eastern Indonesia in this sense, so use 'usually around October to April' for Bali. No monthly rainfall or temperatures sourced (N-106); do not name 'best months' beyond this.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Indonesia: Indonesia's revised criminal code includes penalties for cohabitation, adultery and sex outside of marriage between a man and a woman. If you're married, authorities can act on a complaint from your spouse; if you're unmarried, authorities can act on a complaint from your child or parent.
facts.use_note: Optional context; state exactly as worded, without speculation about enforcement against tourists. Writer and Nic decide whether it belongs in a packages article.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Indonesia consular contact: Australian Consulate-General, Bali, Jalan Tantular 32, Renon, Denpasar Bali 80234; phone (+62 361) 2000 100; email bali.congen@dfat.gov.au; website bali.indonesia.embassy.gov.au.
facts.use_note: The mission with jurisdiction for CNIs for Bali weddings (F-100). Generic consular mailbox, fine to publish; prefer linking.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Indonesia: have at least 6 months passport validity from the date you plan to enter and leave Indonesia, even if just transiting or stopping over; travellers have been stranded, detained, or returned to their previous port overseas at their own cost.
facts.use_note: Country-specific; supersedes the generic F-111 wording for this article.

legal.summary: Per the Australian Embassy Indonesia, under Law No. 1 of 1974 both parties must hold the same recognised religion, or one must convert. Confirm with the Civil Registry Office (Catatan Sipil) where you marry and the Australian Consulate-General Bali.

Marriages are performed by ministers of religion, the Civil Registry Office or KUA, and must be conducted according to the religion and conform to the laws of the parties' countries. Confirm with the Civil Registry Office or the Indonesian Embassy or Consulate in Australia.

Non-Muslim marriages: Notice of Intention to Marry at the Civil Registry at least 10 days ahead, registration after the ceremony; documents include CNI, passports, birth certificates, divorce or death papers and four 4x6cm photos. Varies by province; confirm with the Civil Registry Office of the regency.
CNI from the Australian mission with jurisdiction; for Bali, the Australian Consulate-General Bali. Usually issued while you wait. Confirm with the Consulate-General Bali.
No printed CNI expiry, but Civil Registry Offices do not normally accept a CNI issued more than 3 months before. Confirm with the Civil Registry Office.
PP 9/1975 art. 10: two witnesses, before the Registrar. Confirm with the Civil Registry Office in Bali.

No Australian registration of overseas marriages; generally recognised if valid in Indonesia and would be valid in Australia (Marriage Act 1961, Part VA). Confirm with DFAT, a lawyer, or the state BDM registry for name change use.
Passport in married name: Australian-born spouse married overseas needs an RBDM name change certificate. Confirm with the Australian Passport Office and state BDM.
Legal at home route: NOIM to an authorised celebrant 1 to 18 months ahead; celebrant physically present. Confirm with Attorney-General's Department guidance and your celebrant.
Revised criminal code penalties for cohabitation and sex outside marriage, complaint-based. Confirm with Smartraveller.
